title: Long‑term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity
condition_or_topic: Long-term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)
clinical_background: ROP involves abnormal retinal vascular development in premature infants and can threaten vision. Visual impairment may persist after ROP regresses because of refractive errors, strabismus or retinal changes such as macular dragging and vascular tortuosity. Few studies have examined how these anatomical changes, particularly macular dragging and vessel tortuosity, relate to later vision.
objectives: Assess long-term visual outcomes in children with regressed ROP after retinal management.
Examine the relationships between best-corrected visual acuity and retinal findings, particularly macular dragging and vascular tortuosity.
Evaluate whether gestational age, birth weight and refractive errors are associated with poorer visual outcomes.
clinical_question: In children with regressed ROP (P), is macular dragging (exposure), compared with its absence (C), associated with poorer best-corrected visual acuity (O)?
study_design: Retrospective review of consecutive patients with ROP, examining associations between best-corrected VA after regression and fundus findings, perinatal characteristics, and refractive errors.

population.description: 57 consecutive patients (110 eyes) diagnosed and managed for ROP between 2010 and 2018. ROP had regressed, with or without treatment, in every included patient. Both eyes were analyzed when affected; for unilateral ROP, only the affected eye was included.
inclusion_criteria: Diagnosis and management of ROP, followed by assessment at an age when Snellen VA and conventional fundus photographs could be obtained.
Availability of Snellen VA records and fundus photographs.
exclusion_criteria: Systemic conditions, including neurologic disease, Down’s syndrome, or cerebral palsy, that made VA assessment unreliable.
Ocular structural abnormalities unrelated to ROP.
Missing Snellen VA records or fundus photographs.
population.mean_age: 5.2 ± 1.60 years (range, 2–9 years) at the VA measurement used for analysis
population.care_setting: Retina and pediatric ophthalmology clinics at Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital, Hallym University, Seoul; ROP screening took place in the neonatal intensive care unit.

interventions: Laser photocoagulation with intravitreal bevacizumab injection for ROP.
comparators: Eyes receiving ROP treatment versus eyes receiving no ROP treatment.
Laser photocoagulation alone versus laser photocoagulation with intravitreal bevacizumab injection.

primary: Association of best-corrected VA after ROP regression with macular dragging, the macula-to-disc distance/disc diameter ratio, and retinal vascular tortuosity.
Association of best-corrected VA with sex, age, GA, BW, SE, myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, and anisometropia.
Association of VA with ROP treatment status and treatment modality.

statistical_methods: Spearman’s correlation tests assessed associations with VA. Interobserver reproducibility of retinal vascular tortuosity grading was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients from a two-way mixed-effect model; coefficients > 0.80 indicated almost perfect agreement, > 0.60–0.80 substantial agreement, and > 0.4–0.6 moderate agreement. Analyses used IBM SPSS Statistics (version 22.0), with a confidence interval of 95% and p < 0.05 as the threshold for statistical significance. If multiple VA measurements were available, the best result was analyzed.
follow_up: Patients were followed until Snellen VA and conventional fundus photography could be obtained; a follow-up duration was not specified.
interpretation: Most children in this study had favorable vision after ROP regression, although anatomical and functional sequelae remained possible despite appropriate treatment. Macular dragging was present in 37 eyes (33.6%) and was associated with poorer visual outcomes; a greater DM/DD ratio was also associated with poorer vision. Retinal vascular tortuosity affected 72.7% of eyes but was not significantly associated with visual outcome. Lower gestational age and birth weight, as well as refractive abnormalities, were associated with poorer vision. The authors suggest that macula-to-disc distance may help predict visual outcomes.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The association of refractive abnormalities, anisometropia and strabismus with poorer visual outcomes is consistent with earlier studies, according to the authors. They note that prior research found that mild residual vascular changes have less effect on vision than macular dragging or detachment. In a study by Yang et al., 1.7% of treated eyes had abnormal retinal structure attributable to ROP, whereas 34.5% had unfavorable visual outcomes; McLoone et al. reported poor vision in 10 eyes, of which only three had poor structural outcomes. Earlier studies reported strabismus in 16 to 22% of children born preterm versus 1–3% of those born at term, and VanderVeen et al. reported strabismus in 60% of children with type 1 ROP.
clinical_implications: Retinal structural findings on photographs may help estimate visual prognosis in young children after ROP regression, when visual acuity testing can be difficult or unreliable.
A retina that appears normal does not rule out other contributors to poor vision, including refractive errors, strabismus and amblyopia.
Regression of ROP does not preclude later anatomical or functional visual sequelae.
practice_implications: The authors emphasize early management and closely monitored follow-up for children with ROP.
They call for early visual assessment and management of strabismic or anisometropic amblyopia in children born preterm, particularly those with ROP.
They suggest using macula-to-disc distance on fundus photographs to help anticipate visual outcome after ROP regression.
limitations: The retrospective design may have favored inclusion of patients with threshold ROP who remained under care long enough for visual assessment, leaving relatively few untreated patients with less severe disease and creating potential selection bias.
The authors found it difficult to establish a control group, which limits the findings.
The broad age range of 2.4 to 9.0 years old complicates assessment against age-appropriate normal visual acuity.
strengths: The authors consider the study potentially valuable for examining associations between retinal anatomical sequelae and long-term visual outcomes after ROP regression.
future_directions: Conduct prospective studies with a control group of premature children without a history of ROP.

main_conclusion: Most children in this cohort had favorable vision after ROP regression, although retinal and functional sequelae could persist. The authors suggest that macular dragging, particularly when assessed through macula-to-disc distance, and selected perinatal and refractive factors may help anticipate poorer visual outcomes in young children.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective study examined visual outcomes after ROP regression in 57 consecutive children (110 eyes). The investigators related best-corrected VA to fundus anatomy, gestational age, birth weight and refractive findings. VA used for analysis was obtained at a mean age of (5.2 ± 1.60) years. Favorable vision, defined as 20/25 (0.10 logMAR) or better, was recorded in 86 eyes (78.2%); only one eye (0.9%) had vision worse than 20/160 (0.90 logMAR).

Macular dragging occurred in 37 eyes (33.6%) and was significantly associated with poorer vision (p = 0.002). A larger macula-to-disc distance/disc diameter ratio was also associated with poorer vision (correlation coefficient: 0.200, p = 0.036). By contrast, retinal vascular tortuosity was not significantly correlated with BCVA. Lower gestational age and birth weight were each associated with poorer outcomes (p = 0.007 for each). Larger absolute SE, myopia, astigmatism and anisometropia were also associated with poorer outcomes. Treated eyes had poorer VA than untreated eyes (p = 0.02), but VA did not differ significantly between the two treatment modalities examined.

The authors propose that fundus anatomy may assist early visual prognostication and emphasize early management and closely monitored follow-up. They caution that the retrospective design, possible selection bias, lack of a control group and broad age range limit interpretation.

document_sections.heading: Long‑term visual outcomes in children with regressed retinopathy of prematurity
document_sections.content: This retrospective study examined long-term visual outcomes after retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) regression and assessed relationships between best-corrected visual acuity (VA), fundus findings and clinical variables. Records from 57 consecutive patients were reviewed. Among 110 eyes, 33.6% had macular dragging, which was associated with poorer VA (p = 0.002). A greater macula-to-disc distance/disc diameter ratio was also associated with poorer VA (p = 0.036), whereas vascular tortuosity was not significantly associated with VA. Lower gestational age (GA) and birth weight (BW) were associated with poorer outcomes (both, p = 0.007). Greater spherical equivalent [SE] in absolute value, myopia, astigmatism and anisometropia were likewise associated with poorer outcomes (all, p < 0.001). The authors suggest that these associated findings may help predict poor vision at young ages after ROP regression.

ROP threatens sight through abnormal retinal vascular development in premature infants. Its management has advanced substantially in the past decade. Conventional options include cryotherapy and laser photocoagulation. Laser remains the gold standard for threshold ROP, while the efficacy and safety of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment have been under discussion. The BEAT-ROP trial reported benefits of anti-VEGF agents for severe ROP. Advanced ROP with retinal detachment requires surgery, including scleral buckling or vitrectomy. Eyes affected by sight-threatening ROP can retain vision-limiting morbidity after the disease resolves. A cited study reported a vision impairment (VI) rate of 4.6 per 100 person-years in the very low birth weight (VLBW) population with ROP, with a stronger association with VI in eyes treated by scleral buckling or vitrectomy. Myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism, anisometropia and strabismus can contribute to permanent VI despite stable retinal findings, whether or not retinal management was adequate. Delayed recognition and adequate management of refractive errors can ultimately result in amblyopia. Residual vascular tortuosity and macular dragging can also occur. Temporal retinal displacement, apparent through straighter major vessels and a narrower angle between them, may impair vision. The authors note that few studies have examined how these anatomical sequelae, particularly macular dragging and vessel tortuosity, relate to visual outcomes. They therefore investigated long-term visual prognosis after appropriate retinal management and factors associated with poor outcomes in regressed ROP.

document_sections.heading: Materials and methods
document_sections.content: The methods describe a retrospective record review, ROP screening and management, ophthalmologic and fundus assessments, visual outcome definitions, and statistical analysis.

document_sections.heading: Study design and subjects.
document_sections.content: The investigators reviewed records for 57 consecutive patients (110 eyes) diagnosed and managed for ROP at the retina clinic of Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital, Hallym University, Seoul, between 2010 and 2018. Patients were subsequently followed at its pediatric ophthalmology clinic until Snellen VA testing and conventional fundus photography were feasible. Some had received ROP treatment elsewhere before transfer. The initial review excluded children whose systemic conditions, including neurologic disease, Down’s syndrome or cerebral palsy, made VA unreliable, as well as children with ocular structural abnormalities unrelated to ROP. Children without recorded Snellen VA or fundus photographs were also excluded. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and had Institutional Review Board approval from Hallym University Medical Center (IRB no. 2022-05-015). Informed consent was waived because the review was retrospective and used anonymized clinical data.

document_sections.heading: ROP screening and management.
document_sections.content: Infants in the neonatal intensive care unit underwent ROP screening if birth weight was less than 1,500 g or GA was less than 30 weeks. Findings were classified by retinal zone and stage under the Screening Examination of Premature Infants for Retinopathy of Prematurity. All three zones are centered on the optic disc: Zone I covers the posterior pole within a circle whose radius is twice the disc-to-macula-center distance; Zone II extends to a concentric circle touching the nasal ora serrata, with its temporal boundary approximately at the anatomic equator; Zone III is the remaining anterior temporal retinal crescent. Peripheral abnormalities comprise Stage 1, a demarcation line; Stage 2, a ridge; Stage 3, a ridge accompanied by extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; Stage 4, partial retinal detachment; and Stage 5, total retinal detachment. These abnormalities may progress to retinal detachment. Markedly increased posterior venous dilation and arteriolar tortuosity define plus disease, which indicates a worse prognosis. Aggressive posterior ROP (AP-ROP) denotes severe, rapidly progressing posterior disease with findings in Zone I or posterior Zone II, prominent plus disease in all four quadrants, and poorly demarcated retinopathy such as neovascularization. Retinal examinations occurred every 1–2 weeks until regression and complete vascularization. Patients meeting treatment criteria received laser photocoagulation and/or an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection. Following the 2006 and 2013 American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines, laser was used first-line in the early period before 2013. From 2013, after studies including BEAT-ROP suggested benefits from intravitreal anti-VEGF monotherapy, the clinic began combining intravitreal bevacizumab with laser. The authors describe anti-VEGF injection as less expensive, easier to administer and less stressful for infants than laser. More recently, following the RAINBOW study comparing ranibizumab with laser in very low birthweight infants with ROP, intravitreal ranibizumab monotherapy has been used first-line. Laser is considered if ROP does not regress after anti-VEGF treatment.

document_sections.heading: Ophthalmologic examination.
document_sections.content: After ROP regression, retinal specialists referred patients to pediatric ophthalmology. Children with persistent abnormal retinal findings at age one were advised to attend both retinal and pediatric ophthalmology clinics. Examinations included cycloplegic refraction using 1% cyclopentolate and 1% tropicamide, slit-lamp biomicroscopy and fundus evaluation. Deviation angles were assessed with the alternate prism cover test at distance and near (6 and 1/3 m), across all gaze directions and with accommodative targets; spectacle correction based on cycloplegic refraction was used when needed. The Krimsky method was used for children unable to cooperate. VA was initially assessed with Teller acuity cards. When children could cooperate, optotype VA was measured with a Snellen chart at 5-m distance after optical correction when necessary. Children with amblyopia received occlusion therapy using eyepatches.

document_sections.heading: Analysis of fundus images.
document_sections.content: One of four trained technicians obtained dilated fundus photographs with a KOWA Nonmyd 8S Fundus Camera, producing images of the macula and optic disc. Using an ImageJ scale-bar (ver.1.52) and a previously described method, the investigators measured the macula-to-disc distance in pixels. They outlined the disc with a rectangle and located its center by connecting the rectangle’s corners. They then measured the shortest diameter of the disc’s neural tissue (DD) and the distance from disc center to macular center (DM). The DM/DD ratio represented relative macula-to-disc distance. A DM/DD ratio > 3, or retinal folds irrespective of vessel straightening, met the definition of macular dragging. Standard photographs chosen by consensus between a pediatric ophthalmologist (DGC) and retinal specialist (DJM) guided retinal vascular tortuosity grading: 1 indicated none, 2 mild to moderate, and 3 severe. Photographs were assessed without access to corresponding clinical information. If the initial observers disagreed, SHP performed a third assessment without knowing their ratings. If that assessment matched neither initial rating, all three observers examined the photographs together to seek consensus. The figures illustrate the DM and DD measurements, features of macular dragging and the tortuosity grades.

document_sections.heading: Main outcome measures.
document_sections.content: The investigators assessed relationships between VA and fundus anatomy, including macula-to-disc distance and vascular tortuosity. They also examined sex, age, GA, BW and refractive errors: hyperopia and myopia measured by spherical equivalent [SE], astigmatism and anisometropia. SE was calculated as the sphere’s diopter (D) value plus half the astigmatism value. In the methods, anisometropia was defined as an interocular SE difference of > 2D. The analysis defined myopia as SE ≤ –1.0D and hyperopia as SE ≥ + 1.5D. When multiple VA records existed, the best VA was selected.

document_sections.heading: Statistical analysis.
document_sections.content: Both eyes were analyzed when both had ROP; for unilateral ROP, only the affected eye was included. Spearman’s correlation tests examined associations between ROP and potential risk factors. Interobserver reproducibility of tortuosity grades was evaluated for DGC and DJM using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) from a two-way mixed-effect model in SPSS Statistics. Agreement was considered almost perfect at > 0.80, substantial at > 0.60–0.80 and moderate at > 0.4–0.6. Analyses used IBM SPSS Statistics (version 22.0). A confidence interval of 95% and corresponding p < 0.05 defined statistical significance.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: ROP affected both eyes in 53 of the 57 patients and one eye in four, yielding 110 study eyes; ROP had regressed in every included patient, with or without treatment. Mean GA was 27.55 ± 2.60 weeks (range, 23–34 weeks), mean BW was 1.06 ± 0.38 kg (range, 0.53–2.00 kg), and mean age at the VA measurement used for analysis was (5.2 ± 1.60) years (range, 2–9 years). The results prose states that 61.8% of eyes received laser coagulation alone, 14.5% additionally received an intravitreal anti-VEGF injection, and 24% received no treatment; Table 1 gives a different treatment breakdown. Snellen VA of 20/25 (0.10 logMAR) or better occurred in 86 eyes (78.2%), while only one eye (0.9%) had VA worse than 20/160 (0.90 logMAR). Mean acuity was 0.09 ± 0.20 logMAR (range, 0–1.70), and mean SE was − 1.33 ± 3.19D (range, − 21.50 to + 5.50 D). Of 110 eyes, 44 (40.0%) were myopic, 41 (37.2%) emmetropic and 25 (22.8%) hyperopic. Anisometropia, described here as an interocular SE difference ≥ 2.0 D, affected 15 patients (26.3%). Strabismus affected 15 patients (26.3%): 12 had exotropia, with mean deviation 19.25 ± 8.6 prism diopter (PD) (range, 8–40), and 3 had esotropia, with mean deviation 22.7 ± 11.7 PD (range, 8–30). Table 1 presents demographic characteristics, ROP classification, refractive findings and treatment distributions. Macular dragging occurred in 37 eyes (33.6%) and was significantly associated with visual outcome (p = 0.002). Mean DM/DD was 3.05 ± 0.26 (range, 2.29–5.92); a larger ratio was associated with poorer vision (Spearman’s correlation coefficient: 0.200, p = 0.036). Vascular contours showed no tortuosity in 30 eyes (27.3%), mild to moderate tortuosity in 60 (54.5%) and severe tortuosity in 20 (18.2%). The observers’ ICC was 0.97, indicating almost perfect agreement. Tortuosity was not significantly correlated with best-corrected VA (BCVA). Lower GA and BW were associated with poorer visual outcomes (p = 0.007 and 0.007, respectively); greater absolute SE and anisometropia were also associated with poorer outcomes (p < 0.001). Table 2 presents the correlations between BCVA and clinical variables. The treated group, comprising laser monotherapy or laser combined with intravitreal bevacizumab, had significantly poorer VA than the untreated group (p = 0.02). VA did not differ significantly by the two treatment modalities.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: A cited nationwide population-based study in South Korea reported ROP incidence of one in 500 among newborns and one in three in the VLBW population, together with a VI rate of 4.6 per 100 person-years in the VLBW population with ROP. The authors note the increasing importance of evaluation and treatment as survival after preterm birth, particularly among VLBW infants, rises. They describe a shift from primary laser to primary anti-VEGF treatment as being associated in prior work with fewer adverse structural outcomes, high myopia, cataracts and glaucoma. Nevertheless, residual changes after ROP regression can produce long-term VI. After acute ROP resolves, retinal and vascular structural changes can persist. Prior work describes vascular tortuosity, peripheral pigmentation and vascular anomalies as having less effect on vision, whereas macular dragging, distortion and detachment can cause severe VI. In this study, 37 eyes (33.6%) showed macular dragging, significantly associated with poorer vision; VA also correlated with dragging severity assessed by DM/DD. The authors suggest that conventional fundus photographs obtained early, or RetCam images obtained in infancy, may help estimate later visual prognosis from structural findings. They also caution that VA testing and retinal imaging, including wide fundus photography and optical coherence tomography, can be difficult to obtain and unreliable in young children. Vascular tortuosity persisted in 72.7% of study eyes but was not significantly related to visual outcome. The authors note that strabismus, amblyopia and perinatal neurological events may impair vision even when retinal findings appear normal. Yang et al. reported abnormal ROP-related retinal structure in 1.7% of treated eyes but unfavorable visual outcomes in 34.5%, suggesting contributions from factors such as refractive errors or nystagmus. McLoone et al. reported poor visual outcomes in 10 eyes, only three of which had poor structural outcomes. Earlier studies place strabismus prevalence in children born preterm at 16 to 22%, compared with 1–3% among children born at term; VanderVeen et al. reported strabismus in 60% of children with type 1 ROP. Other prior studies found greater susceptibility to abnormal refractive errors, including myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism and anisometropia, and to strabismus among children born preterm. Previous work also associated ROP stage and zone with faster myopic progression in severe disease. The authors consequently state that early visual evaluation and management of strabismic or anisometropic amblyopia are needed for preterm infants, particularly those with ROP. They report that abnormal refractive errors, anisometropia and strabismus after regression were significantly correlated with poor visual outcomes in their study; Table 2 displays the reported BCVA correlations with clinical variables. The authors identify several limitations. The retrospective design and the possibility that patients with threshold ROP treated by laser or anti-VEGF attended follow-up long enough for visual assessment may have left relatively few untreated patients with less severe disease, creating potential selection bias. The same circumstances made a control group difficult to establish and limited the findings. They call for prospective comparisons with premature infants who have no ROP history. They also note that the broad age range, 2.4 to 9.0 years old, entails different expectations for normal VA. Despite these constraints, they consider the analysis of retinal anatomical sequelae and long-term vision potentially meaningful. Most patients with regressed ROP had favorable visual outcomes, which the authors interpret as supporting early management and closely monitored follow-up. Anatomical and functional sequelae may nevertheless persist after adequate treatment and regression. They suggest that macula-to-disc distance on fundus photographs may help predict visual outcomes and present their long-term data as an investigation of factors associated with poor vision after ROP management.
